query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic HEA subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, the softer phase regions experience wear‐induced plastic deformation that triggers a dynamic phase transformation into an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer (an inverse Hall‐Petch effect). This layer, having a high density of grain boundaries, is more reactive to the corrosive environment, resulting in accelerated overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with distinct, coexisting phases exhibiting different mechanical responses under load.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to combined mechanical wear and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature conditions with a corrosive medium (e.g., oxidizing or acidic environment) and controlled wear loading that simulates service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer in the softer eutectic phase regions, resulting from plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization/amorphization.
generation.mechanism: The mechanical wear induces plastic deformation in the softer phases, driving a dynamic transformation (inverse Hall‐Petch behavior) that results in the creation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer. The high density of grain boundaries in this layer then accelerates chemical attack by the corrosive media, thereby coupling wear with highly accelerated corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline (either a similar HEA without the tendency for dynamic transformation or tests where only one degradation mode is applied), the alloy will exhibit increased overall degradation. While initial wear resistance may remain relatively high (due to the formation of a low-friction ultrafine layer), corrosion rates and total material degradation will be significantly increased.
generation.baseline: A matched material system or controlled test condition where the HEA is either in a single-phase state or is exposed to only one form of degradation (e.g., wear without concurrent corrosion) at similar temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where both aggressive mechanical wear and a corrosive environment are present at elevated temperatures. It may not hold true under inert or lower temperature conditions or in single-phase HEAs with uniformly stable microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent to which each phase contributes to the dynamic formation of the ultra‐nanocrystalline layer and the quantitative balance between the wear and corrosion rates in the accelerated degradation process remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA specimens. One set is subjected to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, and a control set is subjected to only the mechanical wear under identical temperature without the corrosive medium. Use high-resolution microscopy to assess the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer and compare corrosion product formation, wear rates, and overall degradation between the two sets.
measurements: Microscopic grain size distribution and nanostructure characterization
Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Corrosion rate (electrochemical measurements or weight loss)
Surface chemical composition (e.g., via XPS or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion do not show a significantly greater formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer, or if the corrosion rate does not exceed that of the wear-only control despite identical mechanical conditions, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
